newsitem.title: UK: Hebron deal keeps Mideast process alive - press.
newsitem.headline: Hebron deal keeps Mideast process alive - press.

text.p: European newspapers on Thursday greeted the Israeli-Palestinian deal on Hebron as the salvation of the Middle East peace process, while warning that the path to lasting peace would still be long and hard.

Editorials in leading European dailies variously saw the agreement as a political defeat, under heavy international pressure, for right-wing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu or as a sign of greater realism on the part of the hard-line Israeli leader.
In Oslo, where Israel and the PLO negotiated the first Palestinian self-rule agreement in 1993, the daily Aftenposten saw three important messages in the Hebron accord.
"First of all Netanyahu...has come to understand that he must show respect for the Oslo agreements, not just with words but with deeds.

"Message number 2 is that PLO leader (Yasser) Arafat is strong enough to accept a small renegotiation of the Oslo agreements...The third message from Hebron is that pressure from the United States has been and will continue to be of utmost importance," the paper said.
Major French papers praised Netanyahu, saying his signature signalled a new and more realistic approach to the problem than before his election last May.

"What is most important is that (the accord) was initialled by a man elected by people, most of whom did not want it. That is both its strength and its weakness," the centre-left daily Liberation said.

"The fact that this agreement was signed by a representative of hardline Israeli opinion argues in favour of fundamental realism and the power of conviction in the path opened by (assassinated prime minister Yitzhak) Rabin."
The conservative Le Figaro acknowledged the agreement was a compromise accepted by both sides under international pressure.
"The essential is the acceptance by the Israeli prime minister of the political line defined in Oslo. It is the resumption of the peace process."

Dutch daily De Volkskrant said Hebron meant Netanyahu had "crossed the Rubicon despite himself," personally becoming party to the Oslo accords and thus reducing the risk of derailment of the peace process.
But it asked: "Has Netanyahu evolved into a cautious supporter of the peace process? Or was he dragged kicking and screaming over the line under heavy external pressure?"
Dawid Warszawski, commentator for Poland's top-selling Gazeta Wyborcza daily, wrote that, by signing the deal, Netanyahu had avoided new bloodshed.
"At the same time, he has signed a recognition of his political failure," Warszawski said.
Netanyahu came to power in Israel on vows to put a brake on concessions made by Rabin and (former Labour prime minister Shimon) Peres, he wrote.
"Now he has not only signed the Hebron agreement -- the same as that negotiated by Peres -- he has also anticipated conditional agreement for creation of a Palestinian state."
The German liberal Frankfurter Rundschau was blunt in describing the agreement as a victory for Arafat and a defeat for Netanyahu.
"But the premier's debacle is a victory for common sense," the paper said.

La Stampa of Italy was cautiously upbeat. "We're not on the brink of a new war, the negotiating process goes on, even if it's is at a snail's pace, and this is the first deal Israel has signed with Arafat.
"But it would be unwise to talk of a "decisive step' and to sound the fanfares," the paper said
Corriere della Sera of Milan called the Hebron deal "just a stage, not the finishing line in a path to peace that is still long and filled with obstacles".
But it added: "Israeli extremism is now more isolated than ever."

The London Times sounded warning notes. "Both the intensity of opposition within Israel and the rejection by Hamas (the Palestinian Islamic resistance movement) demonstrate the continued fragility of the peace process.
"The main momentum behind the Hebron bargain was mutual fear of the alternative."
